title: Fate of Quantum Magic
authors: Liuke Lyu, Erik S. Sørensen, William Witczak-Krempa
abstract: Magic, a quantum resource distinct from entanglement, measures departure from states stabilized by products of Pauli operators. Such stabilizer states can be maximally entangled yet admit efficient classical description: quantum advantage requires magic. We develop a powerful framework to evaluate the degree of magic in generic many-body states. We use it to study the fate of magic under thermal and dynamical evolution. In the transverse field Ising model, we find a thermal sudden death of magic that saturates with system size, and occurs after the death of entanglement. We reach similar conclusions in generic spin chains, and in the Kitaev quantum spin liquid on the honeycomb lattice, where the threshold shows an intricate dependence on subregion shape. We then study how magic equilibrates after a quantum quench. In quenches of generic spin chains, the magic of a subregion typically dies before entanglement, contrary to thermal trajectories. An explanation is given in terms of the geometry of non-magical states. As a third type of trajectory, we examine the fate of magic with separation with an appropriate notion of non-local magic and establish a sudden death. Finally, we show how to experimentally witness a volume law of frame-robust magic in quantum materials by using neutron scattering.
summary: This work introduces and rigorously studies 'quantum magic,' a resource quantifying deviation from classically describable stabilizer states. The authors analyze how this resource decays in various physical settings, including thermalization and quantum quenches, using advanced mathematical tools. The findings reveal distinct decay pathways, providing new insights into the hierarchy of quantum correlations in condensed matter systems.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fate (decay) of 'quantum magic,' a quantum resource distinct from entanglement, under thermal and dynamical evolution, and with spatial separation.
main_result: The decay dynamics depend on the process: thermal evolution shows a sudden death of magic occurring after entanglement death in some models, while quenches typically cause magic to die before entanglement.
method: The authors develop and apply a framework using the Bures distance to quantify magic, employing advanced algorithms like SOFA for mixed states and analyzing resource decay across different physical trajectories.
model_or_system: The study analyzes generic many-body quantum systems, including the Transverse Field Ising Model (TFIM), generic spin chains, and the Kitaev quantum spin liquid on the honeycomb lattice.
key_observables: Magic (measured by Bures distance to stabilizer states), Entanglement (tracked via PPT), Quantum Fisher Information (QFI), and various witnesses ($\Delta_{XZ}, \Delta_2$).
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), time ($t$), system size ($L$), and preparation tolerance ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The Bures distance is used as a faithful mixed-state magic monotone, and the analysis relies on rigorous bounds derived from quantum information theory.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometric relationship between stabilizer states (STAB) and other sets, showing how different evolution paths (thermal vs. temporal) intersect these boundaries.
paper_structure: The paper systematically introduces magic as a resource, develops tools to quantify it, and then applies these tools to analyze its decay under three distinct physical scenarios: thermal equilibrium, quantum quenches, and spatial separation.
why_interesting: It provides a quantitative, resource-theoretic understanding of how different quantum correlations decay in realistic, interacting many-body systems, which is crucial for understanding quantum information storage in physical materials.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Set of stabilizer states without magic (STAB), and the set without entanglement (SEP). Typical late-stage thermal (T) and temporal (t) evolutions are shown in red and blue, respectively. STAB-first entry is the typical case. The infinite-temperature maximally mixed state is I/d.

FIG. 2. Finite temperature evolution of magic in subregions of L sites in the infinite transverse field Ising model as measured by the Bures distances to STAB. a) Full temperature range. The vertical dashed lines denote the full-PPT temperatures for each L. b) Near-death scaling with cubic fits dB = ax + bx2 + cx3, where x = Tc −T. L = 12 is not fitted due to looser convergence near threshold. Inset: extrapolation of Tc to the thermodynamic limit.

FIG. 3. a Thermal evolution of magic in the isotropic Kitaev honeycomb model for various subregions of a 32-site torus, up to 8 sites. The coloured subregions are the ones that have the most resilient magic against temperature for a given number of spins. b Inset: near-death scaling of magic. c The magic witness WK of the four-site star over the anisotropy–T plane going from the B-phase (gapless) to the A-phase (gapped), Jz = 1 + 2α, Jx = Jy = 1 −α. ¯J is the average coupling. : αc = 1/4 at T = 0. From the Gibbs state of a 24-site torus. At α = 0 the critical Tc for WK is Tc = 2.361 in agreement with a.

FIG. 4. Dynamical fate of magic for quantum quenches in the Ising +J2 spin chain; 6-site subregions are studied. The initial condition is a dimer cover of nearest-neighbour Bell states. For the integrable case J2 = 0, we work in the thermodynamic limit, whereas we use N = 24 for finite J2.

FIG. 5. Death of genuine bipartite magic versus separation as measured with respect to the Bell producible hull, dHS(ρr,B); dHS is the Hilbert-Schmidt distance. We normalise with respect to the distance to the set without bipartite entanglement, d(ρr,SEP). The arrows denote the death of bipartite entanglement.
